key_insight: Generative AI makes idea plagiarism increasingly common and hard to prove, so existing definitions and policies for research misconduct must be updated to address provenance, attribution, and accountability for AI-assisted idea generation.
problem_solved: Clarifies the ethical and policy challenge of identifying, attributing, and adjudicating plagiarism of ideas when generative AI is involved and traditional evidence and detection methods are insufficient.
method: Conceptual and ethical analysis of how GenAI changes authorship, originality, and proof of misconduct
Review of existing research-misconduct definitions and case examples to identify gaps related to AI-assisted idea generation
Policy-oriented recommendations for definitions, disclosure practices, provenance tracking, and institutional adjudication processes
impact: Equips AI/ML practitioners, institutions, and journals with a framework to update integrity policies, require provenance/disclosure practices, and reduce ambiguity when investigating idea plagiarism involving GenAI.
visual_elements: Flowchart contrasting traditional idea provenance vs. GenAI-assisted idea paths (human → idea vs. human + GenAI → idea)
Checklist/decision tree for adjudicating potential idea plagiarism cases (evidence types, burden of proof, disclosure status)
Icon-based guideline panel showing recommended safeguards: disclosure, provenance logging, authorship criteria, and institutional policy updates
Heatmap or timeline showing detectability and evidentiary strength as AI involvement increases
paper_title: Plagiarism of ideas in the age of generative artificial intelligence
